strengths: The core idea—augmenting a windowed-attention/convolutional backbone with an explicit, controlled low-frequency spectral mixing path fused via a non-expansive (convex) bandwise gate—is well motivated by the known locality limitations of windowed self-attention (e.g., scOT/POSEIDON) and by the spectral-bias literature.

The additive, non-concatenative fusion design is simple and avoids channel-width inflation, and the paper provides a clean pointwise amplitude bound (Lemma A.3) showing the fusion cannot amplify energy beyond either source at each frequency.

Consistent empirical improvements are reported across all six evaluated tasks (four POSEIDON NS benchmarks plus two ApeBench Kolmogorov long-horizon variants) with simultaneously fewer parameters and higher inference throughput than the scOT baseline, which is a good practical signal if verified.

Ablations over three components (low-frequency mixing, radial gating, frequency-weighted loss) and an accompanying bandwise spectral error analysis (Fig. 4) give some mechanistic insight into which piece helps most and in which frequency band.

The appendix attempts theoretical grounding (Lipschitz bounds per block, a discrete Gronwall-type long-horizon drift argument, and a Sobolev-weighted defect bound), which is a nice attempt to connect architecture choices to rollout stability.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is narrow: only scOT and FNO are compared, omitting other relevant spectral/local hybrid or multi-scale operators mentioned in related work (AFNO, U-NO, CNO, Geo-FNO, U-FNO) that are directly relevant given the paper's own framing of prior work; this weakens the claim of being state-of-the-art among 'strong attention-based baselines.'

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for any table; all main results appear to be single-run point estimates, which is insufficient for a paper claiming consistent superiority across many tasks.

Internal inconsistency between the main text and theoretical appendix: Section 4.2 explicitly states the spectral mixing weight W is 'unconstrained (no explicit spectral-norm clipping)... which keeps the transform expressive,' yet Appendix A.5 and Proposition A.2's cumulative bound rely on W (and conv/linear operators) being spectrally normalized/projected to a bounded operator norm. As stated, the theoretical stability/drift-reduction claims do not actually apply to the trained model, undermining the 'theoretical analyses' claimed as a contribution.

Ablation studies are conducted on only 2 of the 6 evaluated tasks (NS-PwC, NS-Tracer-PwC), leaving open whether the same component importance holds elsewhere, especially the long-horizon ApeBench tasks where drift is the primary concern.

Reproducibility details are thin: hyperparameters for λ, α (frequency-weighted loss), initial low-frequency cutoff, number of radial bands J, and dataset sizes/splits for the ApeBench-derived datasets are not given in the main text, and the code link is empty ('The code is available at' with no URL), which is a nontrivial omission for a submission.

The paper itself flags an unresolved inconsistency in its own reported throughput numbers (158 vs. 118 steps/s reported under two different, unspecified resolution/precision configurations) without resolving or clarifying which number is correct for the main comparison table, raising concerns about the rigor of the efficiency claims.

The headline '7%-54%' error reduction range is dominated by an outlier task (NS-PwC, 53.6%); most other tasks show much more modest 7-19% gains, so the abstract's framing may overstate typical performance.
Qualitative results (Fig. 5) are explicitly labeled 'not a main result' and appear inconclusive/illustrative only, contributing little independent evidence.

The technical novelty relative to prior dual-branch spectral+local architectures (e.g., GFNet/Rao et al. 2021's global filter mixing, AFNO's low-rank spectral mixing, U-FNO's Fourier+U-Net fusion) is incremental; the main innovations (radial gating, frequency-weighted loss) are relatively straightforward combinations of existing spectral-bias and frequency-domain loss techniques rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: The motivation is clear and well-articulated: windowed self-attention backbones like scOT propagate global information only gradually through depth, and an explicit spectral branch offering immediate global receptive field is a reasonable fix.

The architectural design (low-frequency-only mixing, additive non-expansive bandwise fusion via radial gating, frequency-weighted loss) is coherent and grounded in known phenomena (spectral bias, scale separation in PDEs).
Appendix provides Lipschitz-bound style theoretical analysis attempting to justify stability claims, and the non-expansiveness of the convex gating fusion is formally shown.
Ablation studies isolate the three main components (LFM, RG, FWL) and a bandwise spectral error analysis is included to interpret their effects.
Reported efficiency gains (fewer parameters, higher throughput) alongside accuracy improvements are a nice practical selling point if verified.
weaknesses: Comparison is essentially against only two baselines (scOT and FNO), despite the related-work section discussing many directly relevant dual/spectral architectures (AFNO, U-NO, CNO, Geo-FNO); none of these are empirically compared, so the claimed advantage over 'strong attention-based baselines' is not well substantiated.

Reported error numbers are inconsistent in scale and confusingly presented: the abstract claims 7%-54% relative L1 reduction, but Table 1 and the 'mean error' / KF-Long numbers (e.g., 114.14, 69.89, 31.07) are never clearly tied to a percentage or ratio convention, making it hard to judge whether these are sensible magnitudes or an error in unit reporting.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere; given that several reported improvements (7-19%) are modest, lack of variance estimates undermines confidence in the claimed superiority.

The paper repeatedly frames itself as relevant to 'PDE foundation models' and claims broad applicability, yet all experiments are single-task trained models on Navier-Stokes-type benchmarks only; no transfer or multi-equation-family experiments are shown, so the foundation-model framing is not empirically supported.

The throughput/parameter comparison in Table 3 is explicitly noted in the text as possibly using 'a different resolution and precision configuration' than the Conclusion's restated numbers, which is confusing and raises reproducibility concerns.

The theoretical result (Proposition A.2) showing DRIFT-Net has a tighter cumulative Lipschitz bound than Swin-style blocks relies on an unverified assumption (that the DRIFT branch's operator norm is smaller than attention's), which is never empirically checked, so the 'proof' offers limited practical insight.
Ablations are only conducted on two of the six evaluated tasks (NS-PwC, NS-Tracer-PwC), limiting generalizability of the component-wise conclusions.

The qualitative visualization (Fig. 5) is explicitly labeled 'not a main result' and Channel 0 appears visually saturated/uninformative (no visible differences across GT/scOT/DRIFT), reducing its evidentiary value.
No code link is actually provided ('The code is available at' is left incomplete), hurting reproducibility.
Design choices such as the hand-tuned initial low-frequency cutoff (acknowledged in Limitations) undercut the paper's framing of a principled, fully learned spectral coupling mechanism.
No wall-clock training time or memory comparison is given, only inference throughput, despite FFT operations being highlighted as a potential cost concern in the Limitations section.

strengths: Well-motivated architecture: the dual-branch design (spectral + local image path) directly targets a known weakness of windowed self-attention operators (slow propagation of global dependencies), and the proposed fix (controlled low-frequency mixing with non-expansive bandwise fusion) is intuitive and grounded in classical spectral-method reasoning and known spectral-bias phenomena.

The non-expansive, radial-gated fusion mechanism (Eq. 4.2-4.3) is a clean design choice that provably avoids amplitude overshoot/energy inflation at any frequency, which is a reasonable mechanism for training stability.
Comprehensive ablation studies (LFM, RG, FWL) combined with bandwise spectral error analysis (Fig. 4) give some mechanistic insight into why each component helps, going beyond a black-box comparison.
Reports efficiency gains (fewer parameters, higher throughput) alongside accuracy gains, which is practically relevant for foundation-model-scale PDE solvers.

The paper includes an attempt at theoretical grounding (Lipschitz bounds, Sobolev-weighted defect bound, discrete Gronwall argument) that, while not fully rigorous, shows effort toward explaining why reduced effective gain could mitigate rollout drift.
weaknesses: Only two baselines are compared (SCOT and FNO); more relevant spectral/multiscale neural operators discussed in Related Work (AFNO, U-NO, CNO, Geo-FNO) are never empirically compared, and PDE-Refiner—explicitly cited as the key prior work addressing closed-loop drift—is also omitted from experiments despite being central to the paper's motivating problem.

No error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the main results, ablations, or efficiency tables, making it impossible to assess whether the reported 7%-54% error reductions are statistically meaningful or within run-to-run noise.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A relies on assumptions (e.g., spectral-norm clipping/projection of W and convolution kernels, Kconv ≤ 1, Klin ≤ cL) that are explicitly stated as NOT enforced in the actual model (Section 4.2: "W is unconstrained (no explicit spectral-norm clipping)"), so the Lipschitz/Gronwall bounds do not actually apply to the trained model and are more illustrative than rigorous guarantees.

Table 1 reports POSEIDON-benchmark errors on the order of 1-5 but ApeBench/KF-Long errors on the order of 60-115 without clarifying the differing normalization/units, creating a confusing and internally inconsistent presentation of the main results table.

Qualitative visualization (Fig. 5, FNS-KF) shows negligible visible difference between scOT and DRIFT-Net predictions, which undercuts the magnitude of improvement suggested by the quantitative tables.

Key implementation/hyperparameter details (initial cutoff values, number of radial bands J, λ and α in the frequency-weighted loss, mask learning schedule) are deferred to appendices or left unspecified, limiting reproducibility; the "Code is available at" link is empty/missing.

The method is only validated on 2D Navier-Stokes-type flows (POSEIDON suite + two ApeBench Kolmogorov variants); despite being framed as a general PDE operator-learning advance and foundation-model component, there is no evaluation on heterogeneous PDE families, different boundary conditions, or irregular geometries, which the related-work section explicitly notes as strengths of POSEIDON's transfer capability.

No training-time/compute cost comparison is given, only inference throughput; given the additional FFT operations per block, a discussion of training overhead would be relevant to fully assess practicality.

strengths: Well-motivated architectural idea: combining a global spectral branch (restricted to controlled low-frequency mixing) with a local ConvNeXt-style image branch addresses a plausible and clearly articulated weakness of windowed-attention backbones (slow propagation of global information, error drift in autoregressive rollouts).
The bandwise radial-gating fusion mechanism is simple, well-justified (avoids concatenation/width inflation), and comes with a clean, correct non-expansiveness proof (convex combination bound).

Extensive empirical evaluation: 7 POSEIDON benchmark tasks spanning elliptic/parabolic/hyperbolic/Navier-Stokes PDEs, plus two long-horizon (T=100) ApeBench Kolmogorov-flow datasets, consistently showing accuracy gains over scOT and other baselines (FNO, U-NO, U-Net-ConvNeXt, Refiner U-Net).

Efficiency gains are demonstrated concretely: fewer parameters, lower peak memory, faster training/epoch, and higher inference throughput than scOT at matched settings, which is a practically valuable contribution beyond just accuracy.

Thorough ablation study (LFM, RG, FWL, conv/linear branches) with per-band spectral error analysis that supports the claimed mechanism (RG suppresses high-frequency error growth, LFM helps mid/high-frequency coupling, etc.), lending some mechanistic credibility to the design choices.

Substantial appendix material including complexity analysis, additional robustness experiments (LR sensitivity, sample efficiency, cross-resolution, resolution scaling) that show the results are not fragile to a narrow hyperparameter setting, and reasonably detailed reproducibility information (data splits, optimizer settings, architecture configs).
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis in Appendix A is somewhat inflated relative to its actual content: the core Lipschitz bound and Proposition A.2 rely on an unverified, non-obviously-true assumption comparing operator norms of very different quantities (spectral mixing/conv/linear operator norms vs. attention operator norms) with no attempt to check whether the sufficient condition actually holds in the trained models; the 'proof' amounts to a straightforward composition of loose Lipschitz upper bounds, and the practical significance (does DRIFT-Net's stability actually stem from this bound, or is it explained by something else) is not empirically connected back to the main results.

Comparisons are almost entirely against scOT/POSEIDON and relatively simple baselines (FNO, U-NO, vanilla U-Net-ConvNeXt, a PDE-Refiner adaptation); no comparison to more recent or more competitive spectral-mixing/global-context architectures (e.g., other hybrid spectral-conv models, FFNO, Galerkin/Transolver-type operators) that would more convincingly establish that the gains stem from the specific bandwise/low-frequency design rather than simply from adding any spectral global-mixing branch.

The magnitude of headline gains (7%-54% error reduction) is fairly wide and somewhat cherry-picked as a range; per-task numbers in Table 1 show much more modest gains on several tasks (e.g., FNS-KF: 4.65 to 4.32, Poisson-Gauss: 0.87 to 0.86), and no error bars/variance across seeds are reported anywhere, making it hard to assess statistical significance of many of the reported improvements, especially the smaller ones.

The frequency-weighted loss (FWL) component, while ablated, is a fairly standard idea (similar to focal/Fourier losses cited in the paper) and its contribution, while nontrivial, is smaller than LFM/RG; overall the novelty of individual components (Fourier-domain low-frequency mixing, radial gating akin to GFNet, frequency-weighted losses) is somewhat incremental relative to prior spectral/global filter and PDE-refiner literature, so the main contribution is more the specific combination and engineering than a fundamentally new idea.

The learnable low-frequency cutoff mask and hand-tuned initial band are acknowledged limitations (Sec 6) but not analyzed empirically (e.g., no ablation showing sensitivity of results to initial mask size/shape or to the number of radial gating bands J), leaving open how robust the method is to this seemingly important hyperparameter.

Only one random seed appears to be used per configurration (no mention of averaging over multiple seeds), and qualitative visualizations (Fig. 5) are limited to a single example described explicitly as 'illustrative,' which weakens the strength of the qualitative evidence for the claimed reduction in drift/blurring.

Code availability is only nominally mentioned in the abstract ('The code is available at') without an actual link filled in, raising minor reproducibility concerns for the camera-ready/review version.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage across 7 POSEIDON benchmarks plus two ApeBench long-horizon Kolmogorov-flow datasets spanning elliptic, parabolic, hyperbolic and advection-dominated PDEs under a matched training protocol.

Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of low-frequency mixing, radial gating, frequency-weighted loss, and the local convolution/linear components, together with a bandwise spectral error analysis that is at least qualitatively consistent with the claimed mechanism.

Reports favorable efficiency numbers (parameter count, peak memory, throughput) alongside accuracy, and includes width-scaling, learning-rate sensitivity, sample-efficiency and resolution-scaling studies in the appendix.

Extensive appendix documentation of datasets, hyperparameters, and architecture pseudocode, which aids understanding of the implementation (though reproducibility is undercut by other issues noted below).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core ingredients (low-frequency-only spectral mixing, radial/band gating, additive non-expansive fusion, spectral-bias-aware frequency-weighted loss) closely mirror existing ideas (FNO's low-mode mixing, Global Filter Networks, AFNO-style soft gating, focal/Fourier-space losses), several of which are cited by the paper itself but never directly benchmarked; the contribution reads as an incremental recombination rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A is largely vacuous: Proposition A.2 (the main claimed advantage over Swin-style blocks) is stated conditionally on an inequality between operator norms that is simply assumed to hold rather than verified or guaranteed by the architecture, so it does not actually establish that DRIFT-Net has tighter Lipschitz behavior in practice.

Baseline comparison fairness is questionable: scOT is only evaluated in its 'tiny' (Poseidon-T, ~20M parameter) configuration, not the larger scOT-B/L variants reported in the original POSEIDON paper, which inflates the apparent improvement; other cited strong baselines (DPOT, MPP, CoDA-NO, ICON) are discussed in related work but never quantitatively compared.

No reported variance across multiple random seeds/runs for any table; given that several reported gains are modest (e.g., 7% relative improvement, or FNS-KF 4.65 vs 4.32), it is unclear whether these differences are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run noise.

Some reported long-horizon errors exceed 100% relative L1 (e.g., KF-Long turbulent: 110–114%), suggesting both models diverge substantially at T=100; the paper frames this as evidence of DRIFT-Net's superior stability, but such large errors call into question whether the comparison is meaningfully demonstrating 'stability' versus simply a smaller degree of failure.

The qualitative visualization (Fig. 5) shows GT, scOT, and DRIFT-Net outputs that are visually nearly indistinguishable, which does not strongly support the magnitude of quantitative gains claimed in the tables.
The abstract states 'the code is available at' with no actual link provided, undermining reproducibility claims despite the detailed appendix.

All experiments are confined to 2D, 128×128 (or 256×256) periodic/simple-domain grids; the paper's framing as relevant to 'PDE foundation models' and future 3D/irregular-domain extension is aspirational and not demonstrated, limiting the evidence for broader significance.

The parameter-count mismatch between DRIFT-Net (17M) and baselines (~20M) in the main comparison, while addressed partially via the 0.5× ablation, still leaves open whether the accuracy gains are primarily attributable to the proposed spectral mechanism or to other confounded architectural/hyperparameter differences inherited from the scOT training recipe (learning rate, schedule chosen for scOT, not tuned per architecture).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated architectural contribution: a dual-branch design (spectral + image) with controlled low-frequency mixing and a non-expansive bandwise radial-gating fusion mechanism that explicitly addresses the locality limitation of windowed self-attention backbones like scOT.

Broad empirical coverage: evaluation spans 7 POSEIDON-style benchmarks covering parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic PDEs, plus two additional long-horizon (T=100) ApeBench Kolmogorov-flow datasets to specifically probe rollout drift.
Simultaneous gains in accuracy AND efficiency (fewer parameters, lower memory, higher throughput, faster training) rather than a pure accuracy/cost tradeoff, which is a compelling practical result.

Thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of each component (low-frequency mixing, radial gating, frequency-weighted loss, conv/linear branches), complemented by bandwise spectral error analysis that supports the claimed mechanism.

Extensive appendix with reproducibility details (dataset specs, hyperparameters, pseudocode, hardware/precision) and additional robustness studies (learning-rate sensitivity, sample efficiency, cross-resolution behavior, resolution scaling) that strengthen confidence in the main findings.

An attempt at theoretical grounding (Lipschitz-type bounds comparing DRIFT blocks to Swin-style blocks, Sobolev-weighted defect bound) that, while not fully rigorous, shows the authors engaged with why the design should be more stable.
weaknesses: The theoretical results in Appendix A are somewhat circular/conditional (Proposition A.2 assumes the exact inequality needed for the desired conclusion to hold at every layer) and are not empirically verified against actual trained operator norms (ρW, Kconv, Klin vs. attention norms), limiting their explanatory value.

No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere in the main results, ablations, or long-horizon experiments, making it hard to assess how robust the reported gains (e.g., 7%-54% error reduction) are to randomness.

Baselines are limited to one scOT configuration (Poseidon-T) and classical operators (FNO, U-NO); more recent transformer-based PDE foundation model backbones discussed in the related work (DPOT, MPP, CoDA-NO) are not empirically compared, despite being directly relevant competitors.

All models share the same optimizer/LR schedule originally tuned for scOT; although an LR/schedule sensitivity study is included in the appendix, no architecture-specific tuning was performed for DRIFT-Net or other baselines, which could understate or overstate relative gains.

The cross-resolution results (Appendix G.4) show implausibly tiny variation in error across very different resolutions (4.328 vs 4.331 vs 4.324 for 64/96/128 grids), which is not well explained and raises questions about how the evaluation was actually conducted (e.g., possible interpolation artifacts dominating the signal).
The code repository link is left blank in the submission ('The code is available at'), which currently undermines claimed reproducibility.

The method combines several heuristic design choices (hand-tuned initial low-frequency cutoff, radial band MLP gating, frequency-weighted loss hyperparameters) without a systematic study of their joint interactions beyond single-component ablations, leaving open whether the specific combination is optimal or merely sufficient.
